claims.claim: in Lake of Two Rivers, Ontario, summer smallmouth bass stayed shallow and nearshore
claims.source_value: summer smallmouth occupied shallow positions in nearshore areas, while lake trout were deeper and generally further from shore; on Fig. 3 the bass's summer 40 % habitat ellipse lies at about 0–2 m depth and within roughly 0–180 m of shore (read off the figure)
claims.location: p. 9, Results, 'Habitat divergence: Telemetry'; p. 10, Fig. 3; methods p. 3–5
claims.quote: smallmouth bass occupying shallow positions in the water column in nearshore areas
claims.conditions: Lake of Two Rivers ('Lake 2'), 306.4 ha, maximum depth 41.5 m, mean 14.5 m, a stratified lake-trout lake; fine-scale acoustic positioning array, spring 2017 to winter 2019 (two annual cycles); 17 smallmouth and 17 lake trout tagged with depth-sensing transmitters; positions with error < 6 m for most reference-tag detections; summer = surface water ≥ 15 °C; habitat niche = fish depth × minimum distance to shore, 40 % standard ellipses
claims.note: The text gives no numbers for the bass's summer depth or distance; the 0–2 m and ≈ 0–180 m are my reading of Fig. 3. The habitat overlap of a random lake trout with the bass's summer niche was 0.09 % (Table 2). The lake is large and deep, unlike Hot Brook.

notes: Other values that may help: in winter the bass sat deeper (their winter ellipse ≈ 4.5–7.5 m deep and ≈ 90–230 m from shore on Fig. 3, my reading) over a narrower range of distance to shore, and were much less active than lake trout (mean movement 1.1–1.2 m/min against 3.0–5.8 m/min; summer rates were similar, 3.4–3.7 against 2.6–3.1 m/min; p. 10). Few smallmouth were caught in fall (n = 8) and winter (n = 2), and few of their stomachs held food. The study's second lake, Opeongo, had no telemetry. The source prints the two lakes' coordinates; they are not copied here.
